summary: Defines a new SIP Content-Disposition type called early-session. Bodies of this type follow the offer/answer model like session bodies do, but their session descriptions are used to set up early media sessions, which carry audio or video before a call is answered.

eli5.summary: It lets a phone call start playing a ringing sound or message before anyone picks up, by setting up the audio channel early.

subtitle: A SIP body label that lets phones set up ringing tones and announcements without disturbing the real call's media.

tldr.problem: Early media (ringing tone, announcements, IVR prompts) travels before a call is answered, but setting it up with the same offer/answer exchange as regular media causes problems with forking, security and media clipping.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3959 defines a new Content-Disposition type, early-session, whose bodies follow the normal offer/answer model but set up early media inside the early dialog, independent of the regular session.
tldr.outcome: Application servers and user agents can exchange early media separately from regular media, within the original dialog. A new option tag, early-session, announces support.

facts.label: Refusing an offer
facts.value: Set every media stream port to zero

today: RFC 3959 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2004. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the metadata. It works with the early media models in RFC 3960.

sections.title: What Early Media Is
sections.content:
Early media is media such as audio and video that is exchanged before the called user accepts a session. Within a dialog it runs from the moment the initial INVITE is sent until the User Agent Server (UAS) generates a final response. It can be one-way or two-way and can come from the caller, the callee or both.

Typical callee-generated examples are ringing tone and announcements such as queuing status. Caller-generated early media is usually voice commands or DTMF tones that drive interactive voice response (IVR) systems.

The basic SIP specification, RFC 3261, supports only very simple early media mechanisms, with problems related to forking and security. RFC 3960 describes two models, the gateway model and the application server model. The application server model uses the early-session disposition type defined here.
sections.eli5: Early media is the ringing sound or the recorded message you hear before someone answers. The old ways of sending it had some problems, and this RFC offers a cleaner way.

sections.title: Problems With the Gateway Model
sections.content:
Traditionally, early media sessions were set up like regular ones: an offer/answer exchange where the disposition type of the session descriptions is session. This is the gateway model, and it has issues with forking and security.

  • An application server may be unable to answer the offer in the INVITE. The caller built that offer for the called party and may have applied end-to-end encryption or key management information the server is not supposed to use. Servers therefore need an offer/answer exchange with the caller that is independent from the one between the two user agents.
  • A UAS that reuses the regular exchange for early media can cause media clipping. Some callers cannot receive early media from several UASs at once, so when an INVITE forks they mute all but one. If the UAS that finally sends a 200 OK was muted, a new offer/answer exchange is needed to unmute it, which usually clips the media.

A possible fix is a separate dialog with a globally routable URI. The RFC prefers doing everything inside the original dialog because it is simpler, has no synchronization problems (all early dialogs end when the session is accepted), needs no globally routable URIs, avoids wrongly applied services and makes firewall management easier.
sections.eli5: If the early sound and the real call share one channel, switching between them can chop off the first words. Giving the early sound its own channel inside the same call avoids that.

sections.title: The Early-Session Disposition Type
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new value for the Content-Disposition header field: early-session. User agents MUST use early-session bodies to establish early media sessions the same way they use session bodies for regular sessions, as described in RFC 3261 and RFC 3264. They MUST follow the offer/answer model and MAY appear in the same messages as session bodies, except in 2xx responses to an INVITE and in ACKs.

Two practices are NOT RECOMMENDED. First, putting early offers in INVITEs, because an INVITE can fork and the caller could receive several early answers at about the same time. Second, using the same transport address (IP address plus port) in a session body and an early-session body. Different ports make it easy to detect where regular media begins.

An early media session MUST be terminated when its early dialog terminates or turns into a regular dialog. UAs are RECOMMENDED to use the same codecs in both descriptions when possible, so the remote UA need not change codecs when the early session becomes a regular one.
sections.eli5: The early sound gets its own label, early-session, so everyone knows it is the early part. It is switched off when the real call starts.

sections.title: Refusing, Preconditions and the Option Tag
sections.content:
To refuse an early-session offer, a UA MUST refuse all the media streams in it. With SDP, that means setting the port number of every media stream to zero, the same mechanism UACs use to refuse regular offers that arrive in a response to an empty INVITE.

Early sessions MAY contain preconditions, defined by the framework in RFC 3312, and these are treated like preconditions in regular sessions: no media is exchanged and the called user is not alerted until they are met.

The RFC also defines an option tag, early-session, for the Require and Supported header fields. A UA that adds it to a message indicates that it understands the early-session disposition type.
sections.eli5: If you do not want the early sound, you say no to every part of it. A special word in the call request tells the other phone that you know how to handle early sound.

sections.title: Example Message Flow
sections.content:
The example has two user agents, A and B. INVITE (1) carries the early-session option tag in its Supported header field and a body with disposition session. B replies with a 183 (Session Progress) that has two body parts. The session part answers the INVITE's offer. The early-session part is an offer to establish an early media session.

A answers the early-session offer in a PRACK (3). Early media then flows. It ends when B sends the 200 (OK) for the INVITE (5), because the early dialog becomes a regular dialog, and A sends an ACK (6).
sections.eli5: A calls B. B answers the call request and also offers an early sound channel. A accepts it, the ringing plays, and it stops when B finally picks up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security implications of early-session bodies are the same as for session bodies, since both are part of the offer/answer model. The RFC lists the usual threats and defenses:

  • Attackers who read a SIP message could send packets to the advertised transport address, so UAs SHOULD encrypt their session descriptions, for example with S/MIME.
  • Attackers may guess the address, since many UAs always pick the same initial media port, so UAs SHOULD use media-level authentication such as SRTP (RFC 3711). UAs that want confidentiality SHOULD use media-level encryption such as SRTP.
  • To stop a session description from steering media at a victim in a DoS attack, the UA SHOULD check the address owner's willingness to receive media before sending a large amount of data. This can use a connection-oriented transport, STUN, or the SRTP key exchange.

One risk is specific to early media: a form of toll fraud. If early media is free but regular media is charged, rogue UAs may set up a bidirectional early media session and never send a 2xx response. Yet IVR systems legitimately use bidirectional early media, for example to collect a PIN code. The RFC does not recommend banning it. Operators should consider charging for early media that lasts too long, or stopping it at the media level.
sections.eli5: Bad guys might try to listen in or send junk sound to someone. The fixes are scrambling the messages, checking who is sending sound, and asking before sending lots of it. Operators should also watch for people who stay on the free ringing sound forever.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: Two values were registered. In the IANA registry for Content-Dispositions, early-session is described as a body that describes an early communications session, for example an RFC 2327 SDP body. In the SIP parameters registry under Option Tags, early-session indicates that a UA adding it to a message understands the early-session content disposition.
sections.eli5: The two new labels were written into the official lists so nobody else uses the same names for something different.
